strengths: The paper targets an important and practically relevant gap in mathematical expression recognition: robustness across simple rendered formulas, long/complex rendered formulas, screenshots, and handwriting, rather than only clean or handwritten benchmarks.

The proposed UniMER dataset/test suite is potentially valuable. Its scale, reported length diversity, and inclusion of screen-captured expressions could provide a useful benchmark for real-world MER if released with clear provenance and splits.

Empirical results are broadly encouraging: UniMERNet substantially outperforms Pix2tex and Texify on CPE/SCE in Table 5 and is competitive with or better than specialized HMER methods on CROHME/HME100K in Table 6.

The ablations separate some effects of training data, augmentation, and the length-aware module, showing that the expanded data and augmentations are important, especially for complex and screen-captured expressions.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is a major concern. The abstract says the dataset/model are available but gives no URL, and key details are underspecified: tokenization/vocabulary, exact filtering, train/test de-duplication, augmentation probabilities, rendering settings, and how formulas longer than the stated max sequence length of 1024 are handled despite reporting max length 7037.

The model novelty is limited and not strongly supported. UniMERNet is a standard Swin encoder/mBART decoder with an auxiliary length/counting-style module reminiscent of prior counting-aware HMER work. The LAM ablation shows only a modest gain on CPE BLEU and near-neutral or slightly worse results on several other metrics, so the main gains appear to come from data rather than architecture.

Dataset construction and evaluation protocol need stronger evidence. The SPE test is the Pix2tex test set, HWE uses existing public test sets, and SCE annotations are bootstrapped from Mathpix with manual correction, but there is little discussion of overlap checks, annotation quality, inter-annotator agreement, licensing, or contamination from source corpora such as arXiv/Wikipedia.

Several reporting inconsistencies reduce confidence: UniMER-Test is described as 23,789 samples while Table 1 says 23,757 and the subset totals differ; SCE is listed as 4,774 vs 4,744; Table 3 has an implausible Pix2tex HWE edit distance of 0.004 with BLEU 0.087 without augmentation and 0.775 with augmentation; implementation says training on a single GPU and then four A100 GPUs.

Baseline comparisons are incomplete for the central claims. Existing Pix2tex/Texify are compared, but there is no fair retraining or adaptation of strong baselines on UniMER-1M, no quantitative Nougat/Vary/LVLM comparison despite claims about them, and no analysis by expression length/noise level to substantiate the length-aware and real-world robustness claims.

The manuscript has presentation and clarity issues beyond polish: equations are partially malformed in the PDF, some figure/table labels are hard to read, and claims such as “first study” and “all types of expressions in practical situations” are overstated relative to the evaluation scope.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important gap: mathematical expression recognition under mixed real-world conditions, including long printed formulas, noisy screen captures, and handwritten expressions. This is a useful problem setting beyond clean rendered benchmarks.
The proposed UniMER-Test split into SPE, CPE, SCE, and HWE is conceptually sensible and could be valuable for diagnosing failure modes across formula complexity and acquisition conditions.

The reported results suggest that training on broader formula data substantially improves robustness, especially on CPE and HWE, and the comparisons show large gains over Pix2tex/Texify on the proposed benchmark.

The manuscript includes some ablations for training data, augmentation, and the Length-Aware Module, which helps identify that the dataset and augmentation contribute more than the architectural change.
weaknesses: The technical novelty of UniMERNet is limited. The model is a standard Swin encoder plus mBART-style decoder with an auxiliary length prediction branch. The Length-Aware Module appears closely related to counting/length auxiliary losses used in prior HMER work, and its empirical benefit is modest: Table 4 shows mainly a CPE BLEU increase from 0.893 to 0.916, while SPE and some edit-distance results slightly worsen.

The evidence does not isolate model contribution from data scaling. The strongest gains appear to come from UniMER-1M and augmentation, but the paper does not compare competing architectures trained on the same data, nor UniMERNet against baselines under matched training scale. This makes the claim of a superior framework weakly supported.

The dataset description contains troubling inconsistencies. UniMER-Test is reported as 23,789 samples in text, 23,757 in Table 1, and its subset counts sum to 23,789. The training-set component counts also appear hard to reconcile with the stated 1,061,791 total. These issues reduce confidence in the experimental protocol.

Reproducibility is poor. The abstract says the dataset and model are available but provides no URL. Key implementation details are missing or vague, including image resolution, tokenization/vocabulary, exact LAM dimensions, augmentation probabilities/severity, train/test splitting for newly collected formulas, and how formulas longer than the stated max sequence length of 1024 are handled despite a reported maximum length of 7037.

Some reported numbers appear erroneous or at least unexplained. In Table 3, the HWE edit distance for Pix2tex without augmentation is 0.004 despite BLEU being only 0.087, then changes to 0.775 with augmentation while BLEU remains unchanged. The augmentation markers are also corrupted, making the table hard to interpret.

The benchmark construction raises potential leakage and fairness concerns. SPE uses the Pix2tex test set; HWE reuses CROHME/HME100K; CPE is sampled from the same expanded sources as training, but deduplication and source-level separation are not described. Without stronger split controls, near-duplicate formulas or source overlap could inflate performance.

The comparison to prior work is incomplete. The paper discusses Nougat, Vary, and LVLM-style systems but provides only limited qualitative comparison for Nougat and no quantitative results for several cited systems. The main printed-expression comparison is only against Pix2tex and Texify, with unclear preprocessing and unmatched training data.

Claims are often overstated relative to evidence. Phrases such as “first study,” “unprecedented scale,” “rigorous experimentation,” and “new benchmark” are not adequately supported, especially given the missing release link, inconsistent dataset statistics, and limited controlled evaluation.

The SCE subset is small and annotation quality is hard to assess. It is produced using Mathpix followed by manual correction, but the paper gives little detail on inter-annotator agreement, correction policy, failure cases, or whether screenshots reflect enough diversity for broad real-world claims.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical gap in mathematical expression recognition: performance outside clean, short, rendered formulas. The proposed UniMER-Test covers simple printed, complex printed, screen-captured, and handwritten expressions, which is a more realistic evaluation setting than the common single-domain benchmarks.

The dataset contribution appears valuable. UniMER-1M is much larger and more diverse than the compared MER datasets, with explicit attention to formula length distribution and inclusion of printed, long, noisy/screen-captured, and handwritten cases.

The empirical results support the main practical claim that training on the proposed data substantially improves robustness. On UniMER-Test, UniMERNet trained on UniMER-1M improves strongly over Pix2tex/Pix2tex+HWE training for CPE and SCE, and Table 5 shows large gains over Pix2tex and Texify on complex printed and screen-captured formulas.

The paper includes useful ablations for training data, augmentation, and the length-aware module. The results make a convincing case that the dataset and augmentations are major contributors, especially for noisy screen-captured expressions.

The model also performs competitively on established handwritten benchmarks, with strong results on CROHME 2014/2016/2019 and HME100K, suggesting that the approach is broadly useful rather than narrowly tuned to one test set.
weaknesses: The algorithmic novelty is moderate. UniMERNet is largely a standard Swin Transformer encoder plus mBART-style decoder, and the Length-Aware Module resembles a counting/length auxiliary head. Its ablation shows a clear gain mainly on CPE BLEU, while it slightly worsens some SPE/SCE edit-distance numbers, so the central technical novelty is less compelling than the dataset contribution.

Dataset construction and split details need more rigor. The paper gives inconsistent counts for UniMER-Test and SCE samples, and it is not fully clear how overlap or near-duplicate leakage is prevented between formulas mined from public sources and the evaluation sets, especially for rendered expressions.

The SCE subset is important but under-described. The manuscript says SCEs were collected and used as the SCE test set, while UniMER-1M is also described as mixed and real-world; it is unclear whether any real SCE samples are in training or whether robustness is entirely from synthetic augmentation.

Reproducibility is weaker than desired. The abstract says the dataset and model are available but the URL is blank in the manuscript, and implementation details omit important choices such as tokenizer/vocabulary, image resolution/preprocessing, decoding strategy, augmentation probabilities, and exact dataset filtering/deduplication rules.

The evaluation of printed/formula OCR baselines is somewhat narrow. Quantitative comparisons focus mainly on Pix2tex and Texify; LVLM/document models such as Nougat are only qualitatively discussed, despite being mentioned as relevant baselines. More standardized exact-match or rendered-equivalence metrics would also better complement BLEU/edit distance for LaTeX.

There are several presentation and table issues that reduce confidence in details, including apparent table inconsistencies such as the Pix2tex HWE edit-distance value in Table 3, typos such as CHROME/CROHME and CHOME, and overstatements like “significantly” when gains on SPE are small. These are fixable but should be corrected.

strengths: The paper targets an important and practical gap in mathematical expression recognition: robustness beyond clean rendered formulas. The proposed UniMER-Test explicitly separates simple printed, complex printed, screen-captured, and handwritten expressions, which is a useful evaluation design for exposing failure modes hidden by older benchmarks.

The dataset contribution is substantial. UniMER-1M contains over one million image-LaTeX pairs with broader length and source diversity than IM2LATEX, Pix2tex, CROHME, and HME100K, and the paper gives a reasonably concrete collection pipeline for rendered, screen-captured, and handwritten subsets.

The empirical evidence strongly supports the main data-scaling claim. Training the same model on UniMER-1M improves performance across all subsets, especially CPE and HWE, and the Texify* comparison shows that the dataset itself accounts for much of the gain over prior open-source systems.

The model changes are well motivated for MER: finer patch embedding for small symbols, local convolutional enhancement for superscript/subscript structure, and decoder attention compression for speed. The ablation table isolates these components and shows consistent, if modest, gains plus a clear throughput improvement from Squeeze Attention.

The evaluation includes multiple metrics, model sizes, speed measurements, data ablations, architecture ablations, and pretraining ablations. This makes the paper more convincing than a pure benchmark release or a pure architecture paper.
weaknesses: The architectural novelty is incremental. The main modules are plausible adaptations of known ideas: overlapping convolutional patch embedding, convolutional enhancement inside a transformer, removing shifted windows, and low-dimensional attention projections. The strongest contribution is the dataset and benchmark rather than a fundamentally new recognition method.

The evaluation of real-world generalization is still somewhat narrow. The SCE subset has only 4,744 unique expressions collected from 1,000 PDF pages, and the paper does not clearly characterize source diversity, page-level split policies, or whether formulas from the same documents/sources could leak into training, pretraining, or rendered data collection.

The dataset annotation procedure needs stronger validation. SCE labels are initialized with Mathpix and manually corrected by two annotators, but there is no report of annotation guidelines, disagreement rate, inter-annotator agreement, correction burden, or residual quality audit. This matters because the benchmark is positioned as a new standard.

Fairness of comparisons is mixed. Texify is retrained as Texify*, which is helpful, but several baselines are not given matched training, tuning, or speed settings; Pix2tex lacks parameter/FPS reporting; Nougat appears only qualitatively in the main comparison despite being discussed in the motivation; and LVLM comparisons are not quantified in the main results.

The metrics are imperfect for LaTeX recognition. BLEU and edit distance penalize syntactically different but visually equivalent LaTeX, while ExpRate is introduced but not reported in the main tables. The paper discusses normalization, but does not fully establish that evaluation is robust to LaTeX equivalence classes.

Reproducibility is weaker than claimed in places. The paper says all data, models, and code are available, but important details such as full normalization rules, augmentation probabilities, exact train/test source filtering, tokenizer settings, and the 16M in-house pretraining data are not sufficiently specified in the manuscript. There is also a confusing implementation statement saying training is conducted on a single GPU and then specifying eight A100 GPUs.

There are presentation and consistency issues that do not invalidate the work but reduce confidence: inconsistent UniMER-Test size numbers, table captions referring to augmentation when the table is about training data, typos such as CHROME/CROHME and 'piratical use', and some unclear notation in the loss equation.

strengths: The paper targets a practically important and somewhat under-served problem: mathematical expression recognition under real-world variation, including long printed formulas, screen-captured formulas, and handwritten expressions.
The proposed UniMER-Test split is broader than common MER evaluations. Separating SPE, CPE, SCE, and HWE makes failure modes more visible than reporting only on clean rendered formulas.
The empirical results support the claim that training data diversity matters: UniMER-1M training substantially improves CPE, SCE, and HWE results over Pix2tex-only or Pix2tex+HWE training in Table 2.

The paper includes useful ablations for data augmentation, encoder/decoder depth, and architecture components, and reports both accuracy and throughput, which is valuable for an applied recognition system.

The architectural changes are plausible and reasonably motivated for this task: finer patch embedding, local convolutional enhancement, and decoder attention compression address symbol detail, local spatial relations, and inference speed.
weaknesses: The scientific contribution of the model is limited. The architecture is mostly a Swin-Transformer encoder plus mBART decoder with relatively standard local convolution/overlapping embedding/attention compression tweaks. The gains attributable to the architecture are modest: Table 3 improves SCE BLEU from 0.579 to 0.601 and gives very small gains on SPE/CPE/HWE, while the largest improvements come from dataset scale and training data.

The evaluation is too self-contained around the authors' own dataset and training recipe. Table 5 shows that Texify trained on UniMER-1M already closes most of the gap, so the central empirical story is dataset scaling rather than a clearly novel recognition method.

Reproducibility is weakened by missing or unclear release details. The abstract says all data, models, and code are available, but the manuscript text leaves the link blank. The 16M in-house text-image pretraining data in Table 6 is not sufficiently specified or clearly releasable, yet it affects the reported best results.

Dataset construction raises unresolved concerns. SCE labels are initially produced by Mathpix and then manually corrected, but there is little detail on annotation protocol, quality control, agreement, or error rates. The paper also does not discuss licensing/redistribution risks for formulas sourced from Arxiv, Wikipedia, StackExchange, PDFs, books, papers, textbooks, magazines, and newspapers.

There are inconsistencies and ambiguities in the dataset statistics. The text reports UniMER-Test as 23,789 samples, Table 1 reports 23,757, and the subset construction details do not make the exact composition fully transparent. Such inconsistencies are material for a dataset/benchmark paper.

The evaluation metrics are not fully convincing for LaTeX recognition. BLEU and character edit distance can penalize semantically or visually equivalent LaTeX differently, while ExpRate is introduced but not reported in the main result tables. The normalization discussion helps, but the paper does not sufficiently validate that the metrics align with rendered mathematical correctness.

Some comparisons are questionable or underdeveloped. Nougat is adapted by embedding formulas with random text, which makes the comparison hard to interpret. Commercial or strong OCR/math systems such as Mathpix are used in data construction but not evaluated as baselines. The paper also lacks cross-dataset testing on established benchmarks to show generalization beyond UniMER-Test.

Important implementation details are confusing. The paper says training is conducted on a single GPU equipped with CUDA and then says eight A100 80GB GPUs are used. It reports 300,000 iterations but lacks enough detail about optimizer, tokenizer/vocabulary, image sizes, decoding strategy, and training time to reproduce the results reliably.

The manuscript has presentation issues that affect trust: several typos and naming errors appear, e.g. CHROME vs CROHME, ConvEnhance abbreviated as CN instead of CE, and an incomplete availability statement. These are not just polish problems in a benchmark paper because they obscure exact experimental setup and data provenance.

Overall, the paper has a useful applied direction and potentially valuable dataset, but the current manuscript does not provide enough rigor, transparency, or originality to justify acceptance at CVPR. The balance favors weak rejection despite some practically meaningful results.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical gap in mathematical expression recognition: robustness beyond clean rendered formulas. The proposed UniMER-Test explicitly separates simple printed, complex printed, screen-captured, and handwritten expressions, which is a useful evaluation design for real deployment settings.

The dataset contribution is substantial. UniMER-1M is much larger and more diverse than common MER datasets, and the paper gives meaningful construction details, including sources, rendering settings, length balancing, handwriting sources, SCE annotation, deduplication, and normalization.

The empirical case for the dataset is strong. Training on UniMER-1M improves performance across all subsets, especially complex printed and handwritten expressions, and the comparison against Pix2tex/Pix2tex+HWE isolates the value of broader training data reasonably well.

The model changes are well motivated for formula recognition. Fine-grained embedding and convolutional enhancement target small visual differences and local spatial relations, while squeeze attention targets decoder throughput. Ablations show consistent, if modest, architecture gains and a useful speed improvement.

The paper reports results across multiple dataset subsets and metrics such as BLEU and edit distance, includes comparisons to existing open-source systems, and provides appendix analyses on augmentation, model depth, and dataset statistics.
weaknesses: The architecture contribution is incremental relative to the dataset contribution. The main components are adaptations of known ideas around overlapping convolutional embeddings, convolutional inductive bias, and reduced-dimensional attention, and the absolute accuracy gains over the retrained Texify baseline are modest compared with the gains from data scaling.

The evaluation could be more convincing on independent real-world data. UniMER-Test is newly introduced by the authors, and several subsets are either rendered from similar sources or assembled from existing HMER datasets. Stronger evidence would include external benchmarks or held-out real document collections not tied to the dataset construction pipeline.

Fairness of baseline comparisons is not always clear. Pix2tex appears evaluated mostly as an existing model, Texify is both original and retrained, and LVLM/document parsers such as Nougat and Vary are discussed but not comprehensively quantified in the main comparison table. This makes some SOTA claims harder to assess.

The paper relies heavily on BLEU and edit distance for LaTeX strings, which can misrepresent visual or semantic equivalence despite normalization. ExpRate is introduced but not reported in the main tables, and there is limited analysis of formula rendering equivalence or mathematically meaningful errors.

Dataset reproducibility and quality control details are helpful but still incomplete in places. For example, the SCE labels are initialized with Mathpix and manually corrected, but inter-annotator agreement, residual label error estimates, train/test leakage checks, and licensing/redistribution constraints are not discussed in enough depth.

Some reporting issues reduce clarity: there are inconsistencies such as CROHME/CHROME typos, “single GPU” versus eight A100 GPUs, missing or unclear release URL text in the extracted manuscript, and a few table captions that appear mismatched. These are presentation issues rather than core scientific flaws, but they affect polish.
